The LORD Is Slow to Anger, and Great in Power
thuh LORD iz SLOH too ANG-gur and GRAYT in POW-ur
n. phr. (Nahum's preface to the doom of Nineveh, Nahum 1:3)
Hebrew YHWH 'erek 'appayim — long of nostrils, the Hebrew idiom for slowness to anger, since the flaring nostril was the image of wrath; joined here to g'dol-kōach, great of power.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Nahum opens his burden against Nineveh with a line Jonah had quoted a century earlier as the reason he fled: the LORD is slow to anger. Nahum keeps the clause and adds two others — and great in power, and will not at all acquit the wicked. The combination is the whole doctrine. Slowness to anger is not reluctance born of weakness; it is the patience of One who has the power to act whenever He chooses and does not choose yet. Nineveh had repented under Jonah and had been spared, and the hundred and more years between that mercy and this burden are themselves the exhibit of the longsuffering Nahum names. Now the reprieve ends. The prophet sets the attribute in a passage of storm and earthquake — the LORD hath His way in the whirlwind and in the storm, and the clouds are the dust of His feet — so that no reader can mistake patience for indifference. Two things are held together that men habitually pull apart: God delays, and God does not acquit. The delay is real mercy, offered to the city once and taken; the refusal to acquit is real justice, and it arrives on a schedule set by the same Person who set the delay.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): Slow, not hasty; not precipitate; acting with deliberation. Acquit, to set free or judicially to clear from a charge. Nahum 1:3, patience and justice named in one sentence.

expand to see more

Slow, not hasty; not rash or precipitate; acting with deliberation.

Acquit, to set free; to release from an obligation or a charge of guilt.

Power, ability to act; force; strength; the faculty of doing a thing.

Hebrew 'erek 'appayim, long of nostrils — the idiom for slowness to anger.

Hebrew nāqāh, to be clean or acquitted; here with the double negative. Nahum 1:3.

Key Scripture

Nah 1:2 — "God is jealous, and the LORD revengeth; the LORD revengeth, and is furious; the LORD will take vengeance on his adversaries, and he reserveth wrath for his enemies."

Nah 1:3 — "The LORD is slow to anger, and great in power, and will not at all acquit the wicked: the LORD hath his way in the whirlwind and in the storm, and the clouds are the dust of his feet."

Exo 34:6 — "And the LORD passed by before him, and proclaimed, The LORD, The LORD God, merciful and gracious, longsuffering, and abundant in goodness and truth,"

2Pe 3:9 — "The Lord is not slack concerning his promise, as some men count slackness; but is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance."

Modern Corruption

Divine patience is turned into divine permissiveness, so that the delay is read as a change of mind; or Nahum's God of judgment is set against the God of the Gospels as a lower stage of revelation.

expand to see more

The commonest corruption is to take slowness to anger as the whole character and to treat the second half of the verse as an embarrassment. God is patient, therefore He will not finally judge — the inference that annihilationism and universalism both require and that much ordinary preaching assumes. Nahum puts the two clauses in one breath precisely to forbid it, and Peter does the same in the New Testament: the Lord is not slack concerning His promise, but longsuffering, not willing that any should perish — and then, the day of the Lord will come as a thief in the night. Patience is the interval before the judgment, not its cancellation.

The second corruption is older and still current: Marcion's instinct, that the God of Nahum and the God of the Gospels are not the same, with the Old Testament's wrath assigned to a primitive stage of religion that Christ outgrew. The sentence Nahum quotes is itself the LORD's self-description from Sinai, proclaimed as He passed before Moses, and the New Testament has more to say about eternal judgment than the Old does, most of it from the lips of Christ. The principle to recover is that longsuffering and the refusal to acquit are the same attribute seen at two moments, and that a God who were only patient would not be good.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew 'erek 'appayim, long of nostrils — slow to anger because great in power, and for that reason unable to acquit the wicked.

expand to see more

Hebrew 'erek, long; 'appayim, nostrils — the idiom for patience under provocation.

Hebrew kōach, power or strength; the patience belongs to One who could act at once.

Hebrew nāqāh, to acquit or hold innocent; Nahum denies it absolutely.

The clause is quoted from the LORD's self-revelation at Sinai, Exodus 34:6.

Jonah had cited the same attribute as his reason for fleeing, Jonah 4:2.

Usage

"the LORD is slow to anger, and great in power"

"and will not at all acquit the wicked"

"the LORD hath his way in the whirlwind and in the storm"
